title: General Chemistry Practical I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L introductory chemistry laboratory curriculum: lab safety, common apparatus and their proper use, measurement and error analysis, preparation and standardization of solutions, acid-base volumetric analysis, and basic qualitative cation testing.

questions.question: Before starting any laboratory experiment involving chemicals, a student should first:
options: Taste a small amount of the chemical to identify it
Read and understand the safety precautions and procedure for the experiment
Mix all available reagents to see what happens
Remove safety goggles for better visibility
questions.correct_answer: Read and understand the safety precautions and procedure for the experiment
questions.explanation: Good laboratory practice requires understanding the hazards and correct procedure before handling any chemical, to prevent accidents.

questions.question: If a concentrated acid is accidentally spilled on the skin, the immediate first-aid action is to:
options: Apply a concentrated base directly to neutralize it
Wash the affected area immediately with plenty of water
Cover the area with a cloth and wait
Apply ice directly to the burn
questions.correct_answer: Wash the affected area immediately with plenty of water
questions.explanation: Flushing with copious water dilutes and removes the acid quickly, minimizing tissue damage; neutralizing agents can generate heat and worsen the burn.

questions.question: Concentrated acids and volatile, toxic reagents should be handled:
options: On the open bench, away from any equipment
In a fume cupboard (fume hood) with adequate ventilation
Only after the laboratory is closed
Without gloves to maintain better grip
questions.correct_answer: In a fume cupboard (fume hood) with adequate ventilation
questions.explanation: A fume cupboard extracts hazardous vapours away from the user, protecting against inhalation of toxic or corrosive fumes.

questions.question: When diluting a concentrated acid such as sulphuric acid with water, the correct procedure is to:
options: Add water slowly to the concentrated acid
Add the acid slowly to water, with constant stirring
Mix acid and water rapidly at the same time
It does not matter which is added to which
questions.correct_answer: Add the acid slowly to water, with constant stirring
questions.explanation: Adding acid to water dissipates the heat of dilution safely; adding water to concentrated acid can cause violent, localized boiling and dangerous splashing.

questions.question: Which piece of apparatus is used to deliver precise, variable volumes of a liquid during a titration?
options: Volumetric flask
Burette
Beaker
Conical (Erlenmeyer) flask
questions.correct_answer: Burette
questions.explanation: A burette is a graduated glass tube with a stopcock, used to deliver accurately measured, variable volumes of titrant during a titration.

questions.question: A pipette is primarily used to:
options: Measure and transfer a fixed, precise volume of liquid
Weigh solid samples accurately
Heat liquids over a Bunsen burner
Filter a precipitate from a solution
questions.correct_answer: Measure and transfer a fixed, precise volume of liquid
questions.explanation: A volumetric (bulb) pipette is calibrated to deliver one specific, accurate volume, commonly used to transfer a measured aliquot in titrations.

questions.question: A volumetric flask is designed to:
options: Contain a precise volume of solution at a specified temperature when filled to the calibration mark
Measure the temperature of a solution
Deliver variable volumes of liquid drop by drop
Store concentrated acids for long periods
questions.correct_answer: Contain a precise volume of solution at a specified temperature when filled to the calibration mark
questions.explanation: Volumetric flasks are calibrated 'to contain' a fixed volume, and are used to prepare standard solutions of accurately known concentration.

questions.question: When reading the volume of liquid in a burette or measuring cylinder, the correct technique is to read the meniscus:
options: From above, looking down into the vessel
At eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus for most aqueous solutions
From any convenient angle, as it does not affect accuracy
At the top of the meniscus for all liquids
questions.correct_answer: At eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus for most aqueous solutions
questions.explanation: Reading at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus avoids parallax error, which is essential for accurate volumetric measurement.

questions.question: An analytical balance used for weighing samples in general chemistry practicals typically measures mass to the nearest:
options: 1 g
questions.explanation: Analytical balances used in quantitative laboratory work are typically precise to four decimal places (0.0001 g), enabling accurate mass measurements for standard solution preparation.

questions.question: Before weighing a solid sample on an electronic balance to determine its exact mass, the empty container should first be:
options: Ignored, since its mass does not matter
Tared (zeroed) so that only the mass of the sample is recorded
Weighed together with an unrelated object
Heated to remove moisture before every weighing
questions.correct_answer: Tared (zeroed) so that only the mass of the sample is recorded
questions.explanation: Taring resets the balance to zero with the empty container in place, so subsequent readings show only the mass of the substance added.

questions.question: In an acid-base titration, the point at which the indicator changes colour, signalling the end of the titration, is called the:
options: Equivalence point
End point
Saturation point
Boiling point
questions.correct_answer: End point
questions.explanation: The end point is the observed point (e.g., a colour change) at which the titration is stopped, ideally very close to the true equivalence point where stoichiometrically equal amounts of acid and base have reacted.

questions.question: Phenolphthalein indicator is colourless in acidic solution and turns which colour in basic solution?
options: Pink/magenta
Yellow
Blue
Green
questions.correct_answer: Pink/magenta
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless below pH ~8.2 and turns pink to magenta above pH ~10, making it suitable for titrations where the equivalence point is basic.

questions.question: Methyl orange indicator is most suitable for titrating a:
options: Strong acid against a strong base only
Weak base against a strong acid
Weak acid against a weak base
Strong base against a weak base
questions.correct_answer: Weak base against a strong acid
questions.explanation: Methyl orange changes colour in the acidic pH range (~3.1-4.4), matching the acidic equivalence point produced when a strong acid is used to titrate a weak base.

questions.question: A solution of accurately known concentration, used to standardize another solution, is called a:
options: Buffer solution
Standard solution
Saturated solution
Colloidal solution
questions.correct_answer: Standard solution
questions.explanation: A standard solution has a precisely known concentration and is used as a reference to determine the concentration of another solution by titration.

questions.question: Anhydrous sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) is commonly used as a primary standard in acid-base titrations because it:
options: Is unstable and reacts rapidly with atmospheric moisture
Is available in high purity, is stable, non-hygroscopic, and has a known, reproducible formula
Cannot be dissolved in water
Changes colour on its own without an indicator
questions.correct_answer: Is available in high purity, is stable, non-hygroscopic, and has a known, reproducible formula
questions.explanation: A good primary standard must be obtainable in pure, stable form with a known formula so that solutions of precisely known concentration can be prepared directly by weighing.

questions.question: In a titration to standardize a sodium hydroxide solution against standard hydrochloric acid, 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl exactly neutralizes 20.0 cm³ of NaOH solution. The concentration of the NaOH solution is:
options: 0.080 mol/dm³
0.100 mol/dm³
0.125 mol/dm³
0.200 mol/dm³
questions.correct_answer: 0.125 mol/dm³
questions.explanation: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O (1:1 ratio). Moles HCl = 0.025 × 0.100 = 0.0025 mol = moles NaOH. Concentration NaOH = 0.0025/0.020 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

questions.question: A titration should generally be repeated until at least two consecutive titre volumes agree within about:
options: 5.0 cm³ of each other
0.1 cm³ (concordant results)
1 dm³ of each other
50% of each other
questions.correct_answer: 0.1 cm³ (concordant results)
questions.explanation: Concordant titres (typically within 0.1 cm³) indicate good precision and reliability of the average titre value used for calculations.

questions.question: Before use, a burette should be rinsed with:
options: Distilled water only, left wet
A small portion of the solution it will contain
Tap water and left to dry naturally with no further rinsing needed
Concentrated acid regardless of the titrant to be used
questions.correct_answer: A small portion of the solution it will contain
questions.explanation: Rinsing the burette with the titrant solution itself prevents dilution of the titrant by residual water, ensuring accurate concentration during the titration.

questions.question: To prepare 250 cm³ of a standard solution from a weighed solid, after dissolving the solid in a small volume of solvent in a beaker, the solution should be:
options: Discarded and the process repeated in the volumetric flask directly
Transferred quantitatively into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and made up to the mark with solvent
Left in the beaker permanently
Heated to dryness before use
questions.correct_answer: Transferred quantitatively into a 250 cm³ volumetric flask and made up to the mark with solvent
questions.explanation: Quantitative transfer (including rinsing the beaker into the flask) followed by making up to the calibration mark ensures no loss of solute and an accurately known final concentration.

questions.question: What mass of NaOH (molar mass 40 g/mol) is required to prepare 500 cm³ of a 0.2 mol/dm³ solution?
questions.explanation: Moles required = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1 mol; mass = 0.1 × 40 = 4.0 g.

questions.question: 'Dilution' of a solution refers to the process of:
options: Increasing the concentration of solute by adding more solute
Decreasing the concentration of a solution by adding more solvent
Removing all the solvent from a solution
Mixing two solutions of different solutes
questions.correct_answer: Decreasing the concentration of a solution by adding more solvent
questions.explanation: Dilution lowers the concentration of a solution by increasing the total volume through addition of solvent, while the moles of solute remain unchanged.

questions.question: A deliquescent substance is one that:
options: Loses its water of crystallization on exposure to air
Absorbs moisture from the air to the point of dissolving
Is completely insoluble in water
Sublimes readily at room temperature
questions.correct_answer: Absorbs moisture from the air to the point of dissolving
questions.explanation: Deliquescent substances (e.g., NaOH pellets) absorb atmospheric moisture so strongly that they eventually dissolve in the water they absorb, which is why such substances make poor primary standards.

questions.question: A student adds dilute sodium hydroxide solution dropwise to a solution suspected of containing Fe³⁺ ions and observes a reddish-brown precipitate. This confirms the presence of:
options: Fe²⁺ ions
Fe³⁺ ions
Cu²⁺ ions
Al³⁺ ions
questions.correct_answer: Fe³⁺ ions
questions.explanation: Fe³⁺ ions form a reddish-brown gelatinous precipitate of Fe(OH)3 with sodium hydroxide, which is insoluble in excess NaOH.

questions.question: Addition of excess ammonia solution to a Cu²⁺ salt solution produces a characteristic:
options: White precipitate that dissolves in excess
Deep blue solution due to formation of a copper-ammonia complex
Yellow precipitate
Colourless solution
questions.correct_answer: Deep blue solution due to formation of a copper-ammonia complex
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ first forms a pale blue precipitate with a little ammonia, which dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep (royal) blue solution of the tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion.

questions.question: A white precipitate that is soluble in both excess NaOH and excess NH3 solution is characteristic of which cation?
options: Zn²⁺
Fe³⁺
Cu²⁺
Ba²⁺
questions.correct_answer: Zn²⁺
questions.explanation: Zn²⁺ forms a white precipitate of Zn(OH)2 with NaOH or NH3, which is amphoteric and redissolves in excess of either reagent to form soluble complexes.

questions.question: The flame test for potassium ions (K⁺) produces a characteristic flame colour of:
options: Brick red
Lilac (pale purple)
Golden yellow
Green
questions.correct_answer: Lilac (pale purple)
questions.explanation: Potassium compounds impart a characteristic lilac flame colour in a flame test, used as a simple qualitative test for K⁺.

questions.question: In flame tests, sodium ions (Na⁺) produce a characteristic flame colour of:
options: Golden/persistent yellow
Lilac
Brick red
Blue-green
questions.correct_answer: Golden/persistent yellow
questions.explanation: Sodium compounds give an intense, persistent golden-yellow flame colour, a simple and sensitive qualitative test for Na⁺.

questions.question: Addition of dilute HCl followed by excess ammonium hydroxide to a solution containing Al³⁺ ions produces a:
options: White gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)3, insoluble in excess ammonia
Blue precipitate
Precipitate that is soluble in excess ammonia
Yellow solution with no precipitate
questions.correct_answer: White gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)3, insoluble in excess ammonia
questions.explanation: Al³⁺ forms a white gelatinous hydroxide precipitate with ammonia that, unlike Zn(OH)2, does not redissolve in excess ammonia, helping distinguish it from other cations.

questions.question: The difference between the accuracy and precision of a set of measurements is that:
options: Accuracy refers to closeness to the true value, while precision refers to reproducibility (closeness of repeated measurements to each other)
Accuracy and precision mean exactly the same thing
Precision refers to closeness to the true value, while accuracy refers to reproducibility
Accuracy only applies to volumetric measurements, precision only to mass measurements
questions.correct_answer: Accuracy refers to closeness to the true value, while precision refers to reproducibility (closeness of repeated measurements to each other)
questions.explanation: Accuracy measures how close a result is to the true/accepted value, whereas precision measures how consistent repeated measurements are with one another, regardless of whether they are close to the true value.

questions.question: A systematic error in a titration experiment, such as a consistently miscalibrated burette, would affect the results by:
options: Causing random scatter in the results with no consistent bias
Consistently shifting all results in the same direction, affecting accuracy
Having no effect on the experiment at all
Only affecting the very first titration performed
questions.correct_answer: Consistently shifting all results in the same direction, affecting accuracy
questions.explanation: Systematic errors arise from a consistent flaw in equipment or method, biasing all results in the same direction and reducing accuracy, even if precision remains high.

questions.question: In recording a burette reading of 23.45 cm³, the number of significant figures used reflects:
options: The student's personal preference only
The precision of the measuring instrument used
The colour of the solution being measured
The temperature of the laboratory
questions.correct_answer: The precision of the measuring instrument used
questions.explanation: The number of significant figures recorded should reflect the smallest graduation the instrument can reliably measure, including one estimated digit.

questions.question: A 'blank' or 'control' experiment is performed in a laboratory investigation mainly to:
options: Waste excess reagents
Account for effects not due to the variable being tested, providing a baseline for comparison
Replace the need for repeating the main experiment
Increase the overall reaction time
questions.correct_answer: Account for effects not due to the variable being tested, providing a baseline for comparison
questions.explanation: A blank/control experiment omits the variable of interest so that any observed effect in the blank can be subtracted from or compared against the main experimental result.
